newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK luxury mart booms as rich get richer - JP Morgan.
newsitem.headline: HK luxury mart booms as rich get richer - JP Morgan.

text.p: Hong Kong's higher-end retail and property markets will continue to outperform as demographic change and increasing income polarisation favour luxury markets, JP Morgan said in a report.
"Durable goods sales are not doing well merely because they were previously depressed, nor is speculation the main driver of luxury property sales," JP Morgan said.
"Instead, the fundamental forces driving both are demographic change and increasing polarisation of household incomes in the past five years."
Growth of 5.1 percent year-on-year in the fourth quarter of 1996 was spread unevenly, with the high-end sector performing better.

High-end durable goods sales rose in 1996, while retail sales generally were patchy and actually fell towards the end of the year. In addition, increases in property prices were much more marked in the upscale part of the sector, JP Morgan said.
Meanwhile, consumer spending on services has been rising fast, while the overall figure remains dull.
JP Morgan said the concentration of Hong Kong's population in the peak-age earning range helps explain the focus on spending on durables, services and real estate.
It noted that the 1996 census found that 30-54 year-olds now form the majority of the population, whereas a decade ago those aged 29 years or less predominated.
Also fundamental to the spending tilt is worsening income polarization, with the highest-earning households taking a larger and larger share of Hong Kong's wealth.
The income share of the richest 10 percent of all households rose to 41.8 percent last year from 37.3 percent in 1991, JP Morgan said.
Underlying Hong Kong's widening income gap is the shift toward services and away from manufacturing, JP Morgan said.
Real earnings for financial and property professionals have surged 22-23 percent in the last 10 years, while real earnings of professionals in other sectors have barely budged, it said.
The shift toward a service economy also has favoured a redistribution of income to capital from labour.
Because Hong Kong has no public policy to arrest or reverse the trend toward widening income disparity, the luxury sector will remain more buoyant than other sectors, JP Morgan said.

"The inference can only be that, over the medium term, the upscale ends of its goods, services and property markets are likely to continue to outperform the rest of the economy," the investment bank said.
In the very near future, however, the luxury property market could be hurt by a tightening of mortgage-lending policy, JP Morgan added.
